  1                                  I.   Introduction and Qualifications

 2   Q1.   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 3   A.    My name is James Schichtl. My business address is 100 North Stanton Street, El Paso,

 4         Texas 79901-1341.

 5

 6   Q2.   BY WHOM ARE YOU EMPLOYED?

 7   A.    I am employed by El Paso Electric Company (“EPE” or “Company”) as Vice President of

 8         Regulatory Strategy.

 9

10   Q3.   ARE YOU THE SAME JAMES SCHICHTL WHO SUBMITTED DIRECT

11         TESTIMONY IN THIS CASE?

12   A.    Yes, I previously submitted direct testimony in this proceeding supporting proposed

13         Schedule No. 27, High Load Factor Large Power Service (HLFLP).

14

15                                II.    Purpose of Rebuttal Testimony

16   Q4.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY IN THIS

17         PROCEEDING?

18   A.    I respond to the direct testimony of Scott Norwood on behalf of the City of El Paso and

19         Adrian Narvaez on behalf of Commission Staff. I address their concerns regarding cost-

20         based rates, incremental investments, protections for existing customers, the twenty-year

21         service term, customer-specific Energy Service Agreements (ESAs), the Green Energy

22         Plus (GEP) program, regulatory reporting, and cost-recovery mechanisms. My testimony




                                                   Page 1 of 21            REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                                                                  JAMES SCHICHTL
                                                                                                       3
  1         also identifies areas in which EPE can provide appropriate information without accepting

 2         unnecessary new conditions on tariff approval.

 3

 4   Q5.   DO YOU AGREE WITH THE OBJECTIVE OF PROTECTING EXISTING

 5         CUSTOMERS FROM UNREASONABLE COST SHIFTS ATTRIBUTABLE TO NEW

 6         LARGE LOAD CUSTOMERS?

 7   A.    Yes. That objective is consistent with EPE’s proposed tariff and rates. The disagreement

 8         concerns the appropriate mechanisms and timing for demonstrating cost responsibility, and

 9         whether a tariff establishing prospective service obligations should be withheld pending an

10         analysis of future investments that depend on individual projects and future operating

11         conditions. Cost causation, prudence, and rate recovery for large load customers remain

12         subject to applicable Commission review in the future.

13

14   Q6.   PLEASE SUMMARIZE THE RECOMMENDATIONS OF MR. NORWOOD AND MR.

15         NARVAEZ.

16   A.    Mr. Norwood recommends that a final determination on the proposed HLFLP tariff be

17         deferred until a future base rate proceeding at which time all costs and rate impacts of the

18         tariff can be examined. While Mr. Narvaez does not make an explicit recommendation for

19         approval of EPE’s proposed tariff, he recommends that in future rate cases EPE

20         demonstrate that costs associated with serving “large load” customers have not been shifted

21         to other Texas retail customers, and that all Energy Service Agreements (ESAs) required

22         under the proposed HLFLP tariff be subject to review, modification, or approval by the

23         Commission. [Norwood Direct at 4, 15-17; Narvaez at 4-5, 15-4]



                                              Page 2 of 21                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                                                                  JAMES SCHICHTL
                                                                                                          4
  1               III.    Tariff Approval, Cost-Based Rates and Future Rate Review

 2   Q7.   HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO MR. NORWOOD’S RECOMMENDATION TO DEFER

 3         APPROVAL UNTIL EPE COMPLETES ADDITIONAL INCREMENTAL COST AND

 4         RATE-IMPACT ANALYSES?

 5   A.    I disagree that approval of the generally applicable HLFLP tariff must await a

 6         comprehensive analysis of future costs and customer-class rate impacts. EPE’s proposed

 7         Schedule 27 incorporates approved rates and establishes eligibility requirements, customer

 8         commitments, and financial safeguards needed before EPE undertakes significant

 9         customer-related resource procurement. It does not itself approve future generation or

10         transmission investment or resolve the prudence determination and allocation of future

11         costs. Such determinations must be made in ratemaking proceedings based on the particular

12         investment. [Norwood Direct at 8–9, 14; Schichtl Direct at 3–6.]

13

14   Q8.   MR. NORWOOD ASSERTS THAT THE INSTANT CASE IS NOT THE

15         APPROPRIATE PROCEEDING FOR THE RELIEF SOUGHT BECAUSE EPE HAS

16         NOT CONDUCTED THE ANALYSIS REQUIRED TO DETERMINE WHETHER THE

17         PROPOSED         HLFLP      RATES       ARE         JUST   AND     REASONABLE,           NON-

18         DISCRIMINATORY OR EQUITABLE TO EACH CUSTOMER CLASS.                                 HOW DO

19         YOU RESPOND?

20   A.    As explained in my Direct testimony, the proposed HLFLP rates were developed through

21         a cost-of-service analysis using the same fundamental cost-allocation principles employed

22         for other retail classes, utilizing a load profile reflecting the characteristics of very large,

23         high-load factor customers. The proposed HLFLP tariff carries forward the rates and rate



                                                Page 3 of 21                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                                                                     JAMES SCHICHTL
                                                                                                              5
  1          structure approved by the Commission for Schedule 33A in Docket No. 56903, subject to

 2          the contemplated update for subsequently approved cost-of-service information from

 3          EPE’s most recent rate case – Docket No. 57568. I contend that this prior approval is

 4          relevant evidence supporting the underlying cost allocation and rate design and that the

 5          resulting rates are just and reasonable. The fact that the approved rates were developed,

 6          and updated, based on the same cost of service principles applied to all other rate classes

 7          demonstrate that they are non-discriminatory and equitable. Finally, the Stipulation in

 8          Docket No. 56903 calls for the rates to be updated in exactly the manner performed by

 9          EPE. [Schichtl Direct at 3, 5, 7, 10.]

10

11   Q9.    WHAT DOES MR. NORWOOD CONTEND IS THE PROPER VENUE FOR EPE TO

12          REQUEST APPROVAL OF A LARGE LOAD TARIFF?

13   A.     Mr. Norwood asserts it would be appropriate to delay the final approval of the HLFLP

14          tariff until a future base rate case or other proceeding, so that EPE can analyze and present

15          the incremental cost of service and rate impacts of the proposed tariff and demonstrate that

16          existing customers would not subsidize service provided to data centers and other large

17          customers under the tariff. [Norwood Direct at 4]

18

19   Q10.   DO YOU SEE ISSUES WITH THIS RECOMMENDATION?

20   A.     Yes, there are several. First, there are no incremental costs of service for EPE to analyze

21          until EPE is actually serving a large load customer. And Mr. Norwood’s recommendation

22          would mean EPE has no large load tariff to provide service under. Mr. Norwood’s repeated

23          concerns regarding incremental cost and rate impacts are misplaced and premature. Cost



                                                Page 4 of 21                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                                                                    JAMES SCHICHTL
                                                                                                            6
  1          allocation for recovery of incremental investments will occur in future rate proceedings

 2          when facilities are in operation. That is the time when EPE and the Commission can ensure

 3          that no other customer classes subsidize the cost of serving these new large load customers.

 4          Investments required to serve large load customers cannot impact other customers until the

 5          associated costs are incorporated in rates. Aside from riders, which provide temporary cost

 6          recovery subject to reconciliation and refund, the incorporation of costs into base rates on

 7          a permanent basis is achieved in general rate cases.

 8                 Mr. Norwood’s concerns regarding incremental costs are properly addressed in

 9          future rate-setting proceedings, but that does not abrogate the need for rates applicable to

10          service now. EPE’s proposed rates are designed to recover existing system costs allocated

11          to large customers who are served under the new tariff.

12

13   Q11.   WHAT      OTHER      PROBLEMS         DO    YOU        SEE   WITH    MR.     NORWOODS

14          RECOMMENDATION?

15   A.     Fundamentally, the most significant result of Mr. Norwood’s recommendation to delay

16          approval of the HLFLP tariff is to increase financial risk for EPE and potentially other

17          customers. In the absence of the HLFLP tariff and associated ESA, EPE would serve a

18          new large load customer under the applicable effective tariff – Rate 25. The existing Large

19          Power Service tariff does not incorporate minimum demand or security provisions and does

20          not technically require an ESA. EPE would likely negotiate a customer-specific ESA, but

21          it would not incorporate common provisions approved by the Commission as would be the

22          case with the HLFLP tariff and ESA. EPE’s proposed tariff and ESA provide a starting

23          point for initiating service for large load customers, including cost-based rates and



                                               Page 5 of 21                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                                                                   JAMES SCHICHTL
                                                                                                           7
  1          significant security provisions. When EPE is actually serving a participating customer,

 2          with known load profile characteristics and, potentially, associated incremental costs, then

 3          the concerns of Mr. Norwood and Mr. Narvaez can be addressed.

 4

 5   Q12.   ARE THERE RISKS FOR OTHER CUSTOMERS ASSOCIATED WITH APPROVAL

 6          OF THE HLFLP TARIFF IN THIS PROCEEDING?

 7   A.     No, not related to bill impacts or the subsidization that concerns Mr. Norwood. Obviously,

 8          EPE is not proposing to change rates for other retail customers so there can be no impact

 9          through base rates. As I noted previously, the proposed HLFLP rates are cost-based,

10          reflecting EPE’s most current authorized revenue requirement for retail service and

11          assumed load profile characteristics and allocation for eligible customers. To the extent

12          EPE incurs incremental costs associated with providing a large load customer service, those

13          costs will be incorporated into the HLFLP rates in a future ratemaking proceeding. Mr.

14          Norwood’s expectation that EPE would “analyze” these unknown costs for a hypothetical

15          customer in order to estimate possible impacts is irrelevant to the approval of the proposed

16          HLFLP tariff.

17

18   Q13.   MR. NORWOOD CLAIMS THE DEFICIENCY IN EPE’S APPLICATION IS THAT

19          EPE DID NOT ANALYZE THE IMPACT OF THE PROPOSED TARIFF ON OTHER

20          CUSTOMERS. IS THAT ACCURATE?

21   A.     No. The discovery response that Mr. Norwood includes as Exhibit SN-2 states that EPE

22          did not perform a rate impact analysis for “base rates and fuel charges”. But EPE’s

23          response also notes the analysis EPE provided in support of the EDR rates in DN 56903.



                                               Page 6 of 21                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                                                                   JAMES SCHICHTL
                                                                                                           8
  1          In calculating rates for Schedule 33A, EPE developed allocation factors for a representative

 2          data center profile and used them to allocate costs to a large load rate class within EPE’s

 3          most current cost of service model.

 4                 As explained in the Direct Testimony of Manuel Carrasco filed in DN 56903, the

 5          addition of service to Wurldwide LLC would result in an estimated $38.3 million in

 6          revenue requirement allocated to the data center. The resulting class cost allocation, under

 7          that scenario, demonstrated a reallocation of costs away from existing rate classes of about

 8          $30.4 million – a clear benefit of adding large, high load factor customers to the system.

 9          This same effect is noted in the Oklahoma Gas and Electric (OG&E) testimony that Mr.

10          Norwood includes with his Exhibit SN-9.

11

12   Q14.   DOES THE FACT THAT A LARGE CUSTOMER MAY CONTRIBUTE TO THE NEED

13          FOR NEW INVESTMENT MEAN THAT EVERY ASSOCIATED COST MUST BE

14          ASSIGNED EXCLUSIVELY TO THAT CUSTOMER?

15   A.     No. A proper cost-causation analysis of known costs distinguishes dedicated facilities used

16          only by a particular customer from common facilities that provide service or benefits to

17          multiple customers. The appropriate allocation of costs depends on the nature and use of

18          the facilities, the applicable cost-of-service methodology, and the evidence in the relevant

19          proceeding.

20

21   Q15.   HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO MR. NARVAEZ’S TESTIMONY REGARDING

22          FUTURE CUSTOMER-SPECIFIC OR COMBINED RATE CLASSES?




                                               Page 7 of 21                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                                                                   JAMES SCHICHTL
                                                                                                           9
  1   A.     Mr. Narvaez generally agrees with the approach described in my direct testimony and

 2          notes that future class determinations are subject to Commission review and approval. This

 3          approach is superior to Mr. Norwood’s recommendation because it examines actual costs

 4          for operational large load customers. In a ratemaking proceeding, EPE would support the

 5          appropriate class allocations with known load and cost characteristics and apply those

 6          allocations to both existing and incremental costs. The Commission would then ultimately

 7          determine the resulting class revenue requirement and rate treatment. [Narvaez Direct at 7;

 8          Schichtl Direct at 10–11.]

 9

10   Q16.   WHAT IS THE STATUS OF THE SCHEDULE 33A RATE UPDATE?

11   A.     Mr. Narvaez notes EPE’s filing in Docket No. 59948 and states that Staff recommended

12          approval in the case but that the Commission had not issued an order as of the filing of his

13          October 16, 2026, testimony. I have included an updated Schedule 27 as Exhibit JS-1R

14          with my rebuttal which incorporates the revised Schedule 33A rates filed by EPE in Docket

15          No. 59948. The Administrative Law Judge in the case filed on October 14, 2026, a

16          Proposed Order approving the updated rates for the Commission’s consideration at a future

17          open meeting.,. [Narvaez Direct at 6; Schichtl Direct at 5.]

18

19             IV.    Customer Protection, Twenty-Year Term and Financial Security

20   Q17.   WHAT PROTECTIONS DOES THE PROPOSED TARIFF PROVIDE AGAINST

21          STRANDED INVESTMENT?

22   A.     The proposed framework combines a twenty-year initial term, committed load ramp,

23          minimum billing requirements, termination damages, dedicated-facility charges, and



                                               Page 8 of 21                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                                                                   JAMES SCHICHTL
                                                                                                           10
  1          security established with reference to incremental investment. These measures are designed

 2          to address the risk that a customer delays, reduces, or discontinues service after EPE has

 3          committed capital to supply the customer’s requirements. The proposed security provisions

 4          work together, and no single measure should be evaluated in isolation. [Schichtl Direct at

 5          8–10.]

 6

 7   Q18.   HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO MR. NORWOOD’S CONCERN THAT THE TWENTY-

 8          YEAR TERM MAY NOT BE SUFFICIENT?

 9   A.     The contract term is one component of the overall financial protections. A longer term does

10          not automatically produce better protection if the other contractual requirements, credit

11          support, and recoverable damages differ. The purpose of the contract term is to provide

12          substantial recovery of long-lived investments while establishing enforceable customer

13          obligations. EPE’s proposed 20-year contract term is consistent with standard terms being

14          considered today (See Exhibit JS-2R for a Survey of Large Load Tariff Provisions in the

15          US). Combined with the minimum billing demand requirements, EPE’s proposed ESA

16          provides significant protection from stranded costs. Mr. Norwood’s suggestion that the

17          contract term be tied to the full expected life of incremental resource additions that will

18          also serve the broader system in the future is unreasonable. [Norwood Direct at 10–11;

19          Schichtl Direct at 9.]

20

21   Q19.   HOW IS SECURITY DETERMINED AND ADJUSTED?

22   A.     As described in my direct testimony, the initial amount is based on the estimated

23          incremental investment necessary to serve the customer’s forecasted load requirements.



                                               Page 9 of 21                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                                                                   JAMES SCHICHTL
                                                                                                          11
  1          The annual adjustment recognizes changes in the remaining financial exposure and the

 2          present value of relevant revenue requirements over the remaining agreement term. This

 3          includes the possibility of additional resources being procured in the future, which could

 4          increase the required security. The intention is to provide protection proportionate to the

 5          outstanding contract obligations, not an arbitrary or discretionary reduction in required

 6          protection. The executed ESA and supporting calculations will document the application

 7          of the tariff methodology for the initial security and annual adjustment. [Schichtl Direct at

 8          9–10.]

 9

10   Q20.   WHY DOES EPE PROPOSE CUSTOMER-SPECIFIC ESAS?

11   A.     The Customers qualifying for service under Schedule 27 are likely to differ substantially

12          in requested capacity, load ramp, location, required dedicated facilities, credit

13          characteristics, and service schedule. An ESA provides the mechanism for implementing

14          tariff requirements while reflecting these customer-specific circumstances. Flexibility with

15          negotiating ESA provisions would not be used to override mandatory provisions of the

16          Commission-approved tariff or to confer an unreasonable preference for any particular

17          customer.

18

19   Q21.   MR. NORWOOD CONTENDS THAT THE HLFLP TARIFF APPEARS TO PROVIDE

20          SIGNIFICANT LEEWAY FOR THE COMPANY AND A LARGE CUSTOMER TO

21          NEGOTIATE TERMS AND DIMINISH CUSTOMER PROTECTIONS PROVIDED

22          UNDER THE TARIFF. DO YOU DISAGREE? [Norwood Direct at 11]




                                               Page 10 of 21                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                                                                    JAMES SCHICHTL
                                                                                                            12
  1   A.     I disagree with the premise that negotiation of terms is assumed to diminish “customer

 2          protections”, or that EPE would have any interest in doing so. Mr. Norwood identifies

 3          several areas for “negotiation”, though I would characterize them as simply necessary to

 4          reflect differences between customers served on the HLFLP tariff. For example, the tariff

 5          allows for differences in the load ramp period, which is the time in which the customer is

 6          expected to reach full load. This defined period will likely vary between customers, which

 7          is reasonable, but does not at all reduce the security required to be supplied by the customer.

 8          In the same way, the Initial Security Amount, which also seems to concern Mr. Norwood,

 9          will absolutely differ between customers based on the magnitude of capital commitments

10          required to serve their load. But there is no basis for assuming that EPE would accept an

11          inadequate amount through negotiation.

12                 Mr. Norwood also calls out negotiations around what cost components are subject

13          to the minimum billing demand and the amount and duration of the Facility Charge. Both

14          of these provisions are “negotiated” because they could differ significantly between

15          customers, again based on the type and magnitude of capital investment necessary for

16          service to the particular customer.

17

18   Q22.   DO THESE PROTECTIONS GUARANTEE THAT EXISTING CUSTOMERS WILL

19          NEVER EXPERIENCE A RATE INCREASE ASSOCIATED WITH LARGE-LOAD

20          GROWTH?

21   A.     No. They are designed principally to address nonperformance or default under the contract

22          and stranded-cost exposure. The effect of load growth on rates also depends on common

23          system investments, operating costs, revenues, timing, and allocation decisions. The



                                                  Page 11 of 21               REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                                                                     JAMES SCHICHTL
                                                                                                              13
  1          appropriate regulatory objective is to prevent cost shifting and subsidy and ensure just and

 2          reasonable rates, not to promise that a particular group’s rates can never change. The

 3          customer protections favored by Mr. Norwood are properly considered and applied in the

 4          rate-making process at the time EPE requests recovery of costs attributable to load growth.

 5

 6                  V.     Energy Service Agreements and Commission Oversight

 7   Q23.   WHAT CONCERNS DO MR. NORWOOD AND MR. NARVAEZ EXPRESS WITH

 8          THE ESA THAT EPE PROPOSES TO INCORPORATE WITH THE HLFLP TARIFF?

 9   A.     Mr. Norwood recommends Commission approval of individual ESAs before service and

10          expresses concern that negotiated provisions may weaken approved tariff provisions. Mr.

11          Narvaez identifies potential differences among similarly situated customers, the

12          sufficiency of negotiated security, and the need to review ESA administration. He

13          recommends retaining executed ESAs, making them available on request in future base-

14          rate proceedings, and demonstrating that ESA terms comply with the approved tariff and

15          applicable law. [Norwood Direct at 11–14; Narvaez Direct at 8–10.]

16

17   Q24.   HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO STAFF’S CONCERN ABOUT UNREASONABLE

18          PREFERENCE?

19   A.     The same tariff standards would apply to all eligible HLFLP customers. Different

20          numerical charges or security amounts do not, by themselves, establish discrimination

21          when supported by objectively different load requirements, facility costs, risk exposure, or

22          other material circumstances. ESA contracts will document those distinctions. PURA §




                                               Page 12 of 21                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                                                                   JAMES SCHICHTL
                                                                                                           14
  1          36.003 addresses unreasonable preferences and disadvantages, and the Company does not

 2          contend that an ESA is exempt from that requirement. [Narvaez Direct at 9.]

 3

 4   Q25.   DO YOU OPPOSE RETAINING EXECUTED ESAS AND PROVIDING THEM TO

 5          THE COMMISSION UPON REQUEST AS RECOMMENED BY MR. NARVAEZ?

 6   A.     No. Maintaining executed agreements and supporting documentation is a reasonable

 7          means of facilitating regulatory oversight. Subject to applicable confidentiality protections,

 8          EPE can provide relevant ESAs and supporting information when requested by the

 9          Commission or in a future proceeding. This is very different from requiring separate pre-

10          service adjudication and approval of every individual ESA as proposed by Mr. Norwood.

11

12   Q26.   MR. NORWOOD NOTES THAT THE LARGE LOAD AND HIGH LOAD FACTOR

13          TARIFFS THAT EPE HAS PROPOSED IN ITS PENDING NEW MEXICO RATE CASE

14          REQUIRE THAT THE SERVICE AGREEMENT BE FILED WITH THE NEW

15          MEXICO PUBLIC REGULATION COMMISSION BEFORE THE CUSTOMERS

16          TAKES SERVICE. ARE THERE DIFFERENCES BETWEEN THE TEXAS AND NEW

17          MEXICO JURISDICTIONS THAT EXPLAIN THE DIFFERENCE?

18   A.     Yes, New Mexico rules require that contracts entered into with customers be filed with the

19          NM Public Regulation Commission.            Texas does not have a similar requirement.

20          Irrespective of the difference in filing requirements, I disagree with Mr. Norwood’s

21          assumption that prior approval by a regulatory body of an ESA that conforms with an

22          approved tariff necessarily provides more “protection” for other customers. Parties and




                                                Page 13 of 21                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                                                                     JAMES SCHICHTL
                                                                                                             15
  1          regulatory bodies will have ample opportunity to evaluate ESA’s in regulatory

 2          proceedings.

 3

 4   Q27.   WHY     SHOULD       INDIVIDUAL        ESAS        NOT   AUTOMATICALLY           REQUIRE

 5          ADVANCE COMMISSION APPROVAL?

 6   A.     Prior approval would introduce uncertainty and delay after a tariff has already established

 7          the governing standards. The Commission retains authority to review compliance with

 8          approved tariffs and applicable law, and to consider cost recovery and allocation in

 9          appropriate proceedings. If a proposed agreement requires a deviation from mandatory

10          tariff provisions or otherwise triggers a separate legal approval requirement, EPE would

11          pursue the necessary approval. The Company does not seek authority to waive

12          Commission-approved protections by private agreement. EPE cannot negotiate terms in

13          the ESA that conflict with the requirements of the approved tariff without increasing risks

14          for the Company itself. The protections set out in the tariff and ESA are designed to protect

15          EPE from financial risk by insulating other retail customers from those risks. Negotiating

16          away provisions designed to prevent stranded costs would likely expose EPE to those same

17          costs through disallowances.

18

19   Q28.   HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO STAFF’S RECOMMENDATION THAT EPE

20          DEMONSTRATE THE SUFFICIENCY AND COMPLIANCE OF ALL ESA TERMS IN

21          FUTURE BASE-RATE CASES?

22   A.     EPE agrees that charges and other terms relied upon for ratemaking should be supported

23          and administered consistently with the tariff and applicable law. However, a requirement



                                               Page 14 of 21                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                                                                    JAMES SCHICHTL
                                                                                                            16
  1          to relitigate every contractual provision in every rate case, without regard to materiality or

 2          relevance to the requested rates, would be broader than necessary. A more targeted

 3          approach would provide executed agreements and supporting calculations, identify

 4          material changes or exceptions, and address the costs, revenues, and security arrangements

 5          going forward. [Narvaez Direct at 9–10.]

 6

 7                           VI.    Green Energy Plus and Displaced Load

 8   Q29.   HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO MR. NORWOOD’S CONCERN THAT GEP

 9          PARTICIPATION MAY SHIFT COSTS TO OTHER CUSTOMERS?

10   A.     GEP concerns must be separated into energy procurement and continuing utility capacity

11          obligations. As explained in my direct testimony, participating customers bear all the costs

12          of renewable resources procured under the GEP and energy supplied to other retail

13          customers is valued at EPE’s avoided cost. Separately, Schedule 27 includes demand

14          charges and a displaced-load structure intended to account for the service provided by

15          EPE’s resource portfolio. The existence of GEP participation alone does not result in a

16          subsidy; capacity costs can only be shifted to other retail customers through the rate making

17          process. [Norwood Direct at 9; Schichtl Direct at 6–8.]

18

19   Q30.   DOES GEP ENERGY NECESSARILY ELIMINATE EPE’S CAPACITY OBLIGATION?

20   A.     No. Energy delivered from a renewable resource and dependable capacity available when

21          the customer requires service are different products. The amount of capacity EPE must

22          maintain depends on the contractual arrangement, coincident load, resource availability,

23          and system reliability requirements. A defensible assessment of cost shifting should

24          consider both the energy and capacity dimensions rather than assume that an energy offset

                                                Page 15 of 21                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                                                                     JAMES SCHICHTL
                                                                                                             17
  1          eliminates all utility obligations. EPE has the obligation to plan resources that are adequate

 2          for reliable retail service to all customers without over-procuring capacity.

 3

 4             VII.    Hold-Harmless Proposal, Reporting, and Cost-Recovery Riders

 5   Q31.   MR. NORWOOD RECOMMENDS THREE CONDITIONS FOR APPROVAL OF THE

 6          REQUESTED HLFLP TARIFF. WHAT ARE THEY? DO YOU BELIEVE THAT

 7          THESE CONDITIONS ARE NECESSARY?

 8   A.     Mr. Norwood first recommends that EPE be required to hold its retail customers

 9          “harmless” from incremental costs of serving customers under the HLFLP tariff. Mr.

10          Norwood does not explain what that means, only that the “condition should place the

11          burden of that showing on EPE.” He goes on to say that the detailed mechanics of the

12          “hold harmless,” including the method for identifying incremental costs and the amounts

13          of any resulting rate adjustment or refund can be addressed in those future proceedings on

14          a full record. This condition seems to suggest that costs should not be allocated to retail

15          customers at a future rate proceeding without a demonstration that the allocation is

16          appropriate based on cost causation principles. If that is the case, the condition is

17          unnecessary, because that is the standard practice in a ratemaking proceeding.

18

19   Q32.   HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO MR. NORWOOD’S OBSERVATIONS REGARDING

20          THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S RATEPAYER PROTECTION PLEDGE ("RPP")

21          AND TEXAS GOVERNOR GREG ABBOTT’S JUNE 2026 LETTER TO THE PUC

22          AND ERCOT?




                                                Page 16 of 21                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                                                                     JAMES SCHICHTL
                                                                                                             18
  1   A.     EPE has consistently supported the position that all customers should pay the cost of the

 2          service provided them, and that position is consistent with the high-level statements at the

 3          federal and state level. As with Mr. Norwood’s “hold harmless” recommendation, these

 4          high-level statements are very light on detail. EPE intends that the questions of cost

 5          allocation and subsidy are properly answered in ratemaking proceedings, where EPE will
